seo_title: EagleView vs Matterport for Insurance Claims: Which Wins?
meta_description: EagleView vs Matterport for insurance claims: compare roof measurements with 3D interior documentation and when to use each tool.
h1: EagleView vs Matterport for Insurance Claims
primary_keyword: EagleView vs Matterport for insurance claims
excerpt: EagleView measures roofs from the air; Matterport captures a measurable 3D record of interiors. Learn which one supports your insurance claim and when to use both.
key_takeaways: EagleView measures roofs; it does not document damage itself.
Matterport preserves interior conditions and measurements before repairs.
Roof quantity disputes favor EagleView; water and fire claims favor Matterport.
Large or disputed claims often benefit from using both tools together.
body_html:
EagleView vs Matterport for insurance claims comes down to what you need to prove. EagleView produces aerial roof measurement reports: squares, pitch, ridges, valleys and edges. Matterport creates a measurable 3D walkthrough of interiors and accessible exteriors. Roof quantity disputes favor EagleView; interior, water and fire damage favor Matterport. Many strong claims use both.

Property claims are won or lost on documentation. Two tools come up again and again when Texas property owners, contractors and appraisers build that documentation. They are not competitors so much as complements, and understanding where each one fits helps you build a stronger file before a dispute reaches appraisal.

What is EagleView and how does it work?

EagleView is an aerial imagery and roof measurement service. It uses high-resolution imagery captured from aircraft and other platforms to calculate roof geometry, then delivers a report that contractors and carriers use to build estimates.

What an EagleView report typically includes

  • Total roof area and number of squares.
  • Pitch for each roof facet.
  • Linear feet of ridges, hips, valleys, rakes and eaves.
  • Diagrams labeling each facet and measurement.
  • Suggested waste percentages for estimating.

Carriers, roofing contractors and estimators rely on these reports because they are fast and consistent, and they do not require anyone to climb the roof. For a broader look at aerial and drone options, see our post on drones for insurance roof inspections.

What EagleView does not show

A measurement report is not a damage report. EagleView tells you how big the roof is, not how many hail fractures are on each slope. Imagery may also predate the storm, may miss small features, and cannot see interior conditions at all.

How accurate are aerial roof measurements?

Aerial measurements are generally reliable for straightforward roofs, but accuracy can drop on complex designs, heavily treed lots, or roofs with many small facets and dormers. Imagery dates matter too: an older image may not reflect additions or recent roof changes. When a measurement decides a large part of the claim, it is worth spot-checking a few dimensions in the field.

What is Matterport and how is it used on claims?

Matterport is a 3D capture platform. A camera or compatible device takes a series of scans that the software stitches into a "digital twin" of the property. Viewers can walk through rooms, measure walls and openings, and view a dollhouse or floor plan. Our explainer on what Matterport is covers the basics in more detail.

What a Matterport model typically includes

  • An immersive walkthrough of every captured room.
  • Dollhouse and floor plan views showing layout.
  • Point-to-point measurements of walls, ceilings, openings and cabinets.
  • Tags and notes pinned to specific damage.
  • A time-stamped record of conditions before repairs or demolition.

Adjusters, restoration contractors, public adjusters and appraisers use Matterport to preserve interior damage and to let reviewers inspect rooms remotely.

EagleView vs Matterport: key differences at a glance

Primary purposeRoof and exterior measurements3D interior and exterior documentation

Interior documentationNoneStrong: walkthrough, dimensions, tagged damage

Best evidence forQuantity and measurement disputesScope, condition and causation disputes
Requires site visitNoYes

Which is better for roof damage claims?

For pure roof quantities, EagleView usually wins. If a carrier estimate shows 28 squares and your roof is closer to 34, an aerial measurement report is the cleanest way to prove it. Missing ridge, hip and valley footage also shows up quickly.

But roof claims are rarely just about size. The bigger disputes are about whether hail or wind actually damaged the roof, whether the roof can be repaired, and whether interior water damage is storm-related. Matterport helps with the interior side of that story by preserving ceiling stains, attic decking, and wet insulation tied to roof openings.

Hail and wind claims

For hail claims, close-up photos with test squares remain the core damage evidence, supported by EagleView measurements for quantities. For wind claims, Matterport can document displaced materials and resulting interior leaks across the house. Measurement accuracy also feeds directly into waste factor; see roof measurements for insurance claims for how errors compound.

Hurricane claims on the Texas coast

Along the Gulf Coast, from Corpus Christi to Galveston and Beaumont, hurricane claims often combine roof damage, wind-driven rain and interior water loss. Both tools are useful here: EagleView for the roof and exterior footprint, Matterport for the interior before mitigation crews remove drywall and flooring.

Roof replacement disputes

When a carrier offers a repair and the policyholder believes the roof needs replacement, measurements alone will not resolve it. The deciding evidence is usually the number and distribution of damaged shingles or tiles per slope, the brittleness of the material, and whether repairs can match. EagleView supplies the denominator: how many squares each slope contains. Field photos supply the numerator. Together they let an appraiser show, slope by slope, why a spot repair does not restore the roof.

A measurement report also helps once replacement is agreed. Replacement scope depends on accurate quantities for underlayment, drip edge, starter, ridge cap and valley metal. Small measurement errors multiply across those items, and the difference can be significant on a large or complex roof.

Which works better for water and fire damage claims?

Matterport is the clear choice for interior losses. EagleView offers little value when the damage is inside the house.

Water damage

Water claims move fast. Mitigation contractors often remove baseboards, drywall and flooring within days. Once that happens, the original condition is gone. A Matterport scan taken before demolition preserves the extent of staining, swelling and affected rooms, and its measurements support drywall, paint and flooring quantities. Pairing the model with moisture readings and dry-out logs creates a strong record.

Fire and smoke damage

Fire losses involve char, soot migration and smoke damage that can extend well beyond the burned room. A 3D model lets reviewers see how damage spread through the structure. For commercial buildings, it also captures contents, fixtures and layout before debris removal. Read more in our guide to commercial fire damage insurance claims.

Tip: Capture the property before any demolition, cleanup or tarping changes what is visible. Evidence that no longer exists is very hard to recreate during appraisal.

How insurance appraisers use EagleView and Matterport

On an appraisal, the goal is a clear, defensible amount of loss. Each tool supports a different part of that work.

Using EagleView reports

  • Verifying the roof area and squares in the carrier's estimate.
  • Catching missing linear items such as starter, drip edge, ridge cap and valley metal.
  • Confirming pitch, which drives steep charges and labor.
  • Supporting the waste factor applied to replacement.

Using Matterport models

  • Reviewing damaged rooms remotely and repeatedly without return visits.
  • Measuring walls, ceilings and openings to check quantities.
  • Preserving pre-repair conditions for the other appraiser and umpire.
  • Presenting evidence clearly during negotiations and umpire submissions.

When the other side disputes a quantity, a measurement record usually settles it quickly. That leaves more time for the harder questions: scope, repair method and pricing. Those numbers ultimately flow into a line-item Xactimate estimate.

Strengths and limitations of each tool

AdvantagesLimitations
EagleViewFast, no roof access needed, consistent measurements, widely accepted by carriers and contractorsNo damage detail, imagery may predate the storm, no interior data, tree cover and complex roofs can affect accuracy
MatterportComplete interior record, measurable, shareable, preserves conditions before repairsRequires a site visit, limited roof-top data, large or dark spaces take longer to capture

Costs for both vary by provider, property size and report type, so get a quote for your specific property. On a large or disputed claim, documentation that resolves even one major disagreement often justifies its cost.

Can EagleView and Matterport be used together?

Yes, and on larger or disputed Texas claims they often should be. A practical documentation plan looks like this:

  1. Exterior: order an aerial measurement report and take close-up photos of roof damage with test squares.
  2. Interior: capture a 3D model of affected rooms, attic and any water or smoke damage before repairs.
  3. Supporting data: add moisture readings, weather data for the storm date, and contractor notes.
  4. Estimate: build a line-item estimate tied to both sources so every quantity has a backing measurement.

Combined, the two tools answer the questions an umpire will ask: how big is it, what was damaged, and what did it look like before anyone touched it. Our claim documentation checklist walks through the other items to gather.

Which tool is better for your claim?

  • Roof-only claims with quantity disputes: EagleView, plus damage photos.
  • Interior water, fire or smoke claims: Matterport.
  • Commercial properties: usually both, given the size and number of building systems.
  • Insurance appraisal cases: both, because the panel needs quantities and conditions.

Next steps: build documentation that holds up

The best tool is the one that answers the specific disagreement on your claim. If the carrier's numbers are off on roof size, start with measurements. If the dispute is about what happened inside the house, preserve it in 3D before it is gone.

Whatever tools you use, keep the raw files. Save the original measurement report as a PDF, keep the share link and download options for any 3D model, and store photos with their original date stamps. If the claim moves into appraisal, the other appraiser and the umpire will want to see source material, not screenshots. Organized, original evidence makes it easier for everyone to verify quantities and focus on the real disagreement.

faqs.q: Do insurance companies accept EagleView reports?
faqs.a: Many carriers and contractors use EagleView or similar aerial measurement reports to build roof estimates, so they are widely familiar. Acceptance still depends on the claim. If the report predates the storm, misses roof features, or conflicts with field measurements, the other side may challenge it. Field verification of key measurements makes the report more persuasive.

faqs.q: Can Matterport measure a roof for an insurance claim?
faqs.a: Matterport is designed mainly for interiors and accessible exterior areas, so it is not a substitute for an aerial roof measurement report. It can document attic conditions, interior leaks and some exterior elevations. For roof squares, pitch and linear footage, an aerial report or hand measurements remain the standard.

faqs.q: Is a Matterport scan useful if repairs have already started?
faqs.a: It still helps, but less. A scan captures whatever exists at the moment of capture, so damage removed during mitigation is not shown. If demolition has started, scan what remains and pair it with earlier photos, moisture logs and contractor notes. The earlier the capture, the more valuable it is during an appraisal.

faqs.q: Which documentation do appraisers prefer during an insurance appraisal?
faqs.a: Appraisers want evidence that answers the disputed question. For roof size and quantities, measurement reports are most useful. For interior scope and pre-repair condition, 3D models and dated photos are most useful. On larger claims, an appraiser typically combines both with a line-item estimate so the umpire can verify each quantity.
